solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Rue passion running wild in Jane Austen's work

indicators.note: something running wild is out of control, so the letters before it lose their order

parts.note: the ten letters of the two words are the raw material

explanation.surface: A reader regrets the passions that run riot in one of Austen's novels.
explanation.definitionFit: Persuasion is the title of Jane Austen's last completed novel, published in 1817.

clue.text: A lot of old bread brought up for Picasso, say

indicators.note: in a down clue, bringing something up means reading it from the bottom, so the letters run backwards
a lot of something is most but not all of it, so the next word loses its final letter

parts.note: taken as written, before its last letter goes
a bap is a soft British bread roll

explanation.surface: Someone hauls up a stale loaf, apparently for the painter.
explanation.walkthrough: Most of OLD is OL; add BAP to get OLBAP, then turn it upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: Pablo is the first name of Picasso, and 'say' marks him as one example of anyone so called.

clue.text: Footballers, those on the blue side hoping to defeat the Reds

definitions.meaning: first meaning: wide attacking players on the right flank of a team

definitions.text: those on the blue side hoping to defeat the Reds
definitions.meaning: second meaning: political conservatives, whose British colour is blue, opposing the red of Labour and socialists

explanation.surface: Football fans in blue shirts hope to beat a red-shirted rival side.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a match between blues and reds; in British politics blue is the Conservative colour and red the Labour one.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names both wide forwards on a pitch and people holding conservative political views.

clue.text: Cancel a Parisian party

parts.note: un is the French word for a
a do is an informal word for a party

explanation.surface: Someone calls off a French friend's party.
explanation.definitionFit: To reverse or reverse out an action is to nullify it, a direct verb synonym.

clue.text: Wet turf above animal's lair

parts.note: a sod is a piece of turf
a den is a wild animal's lair

explanation.surface: Damp grass covers the roof of a creature's burrow.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'above' just places the first piece over the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Sodden means soaked through, a stronger adjective for thoroughly damp.

clue.text: More vino ordered for unfussy consumer

indicators.note: ordered means arranged, so the letters are put into a new sequence

parts.note: the eight letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A diner who will eat anything orders another glass of wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ordered' reads as asking a waiter for more wine, but it is the rearranging signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An omnivore eats both plants and meat, so it is a creature that is not picky about food.

clue.text: Suggestions of corrupt politicians pocketing millions

indicators.note: to pocket something is to take it inside, so one piece goes into the other
corrupt means spoiled or perverted, so the following word is jumbled

parts.note: the eleven letters to be rearranged
M is the abbreviation for million

explanation.surface: There are hints that crooked politicians are pocketing millions.
explanation.definitionFit: Implications are things hinted at or implied rather than stated outright, the same plural noun sense.

clue.text: Stick of jade uncovered in this place

indicators.note: uncovered means stripped of its outer layer, so the word loses its first and last letters

parts.note: the inner letters of the word
here means in this place

explanation.surface: A rod made of jade has been dug up at this site.
explanation.definitionFit: To adhere is to cling or remain attached, the verb sense of stick.

clue.text: Reportedly get hold of father's capital

indicators.note: reportedly means as said by others, so the words are judged by how they are spoken

parts.note: bag is to get hold of, and dad is father

explanation.surface: Rumour says someone has seized their father's money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital' looks like money in the surface, but here it means a capital city.
explanation.definitionFit: Baghdad is the capital city of Iraq, an example of a national seat of government.

clue.text: Wanderer, sane in Glasgow?

wordplay.note: in Scottish speech no is used for not

explanation.surface: A traveller in Glasgow turns out to be perfectly level-headed.
explanation.walkthrough: Glasgow is in Scotland, where 'no' commonly replaces 'not', so 'not mad' becomes NO MAD.
explanation.definitionFit: A nomad roams from place to place with no fixed home, so is a wanderer.

clue.text: Swear word from husband on go-kart at regular intervals

indicators.note: in an across answer, one thing on another sits after it, so the husband goes second
taking letters at regular intervals means using every second one of the word

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters
H is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: A man at a go-kart track lets slip a curse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swear word' suggests a rude word, but it means a solemn promise; 'on' puts the husband after the other letters in an across answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An oath is a formal sworn promise, literally a word given when one swears.

clue.text: US novelist from outskirts of Maine left French town

indicators.note: the outskirts are the edges, so only the first and last letters are kept

parts.note: the edge letters of the state's name
L is the abbreviation for left
ville is the French word for town

explanation.surface: An American writer moved from Maine and left for a town in France.
explanation.definitionFit: Herman Melville was the nineteenth-century American author of Moby-Dick.

clue.text: Some splendid act I cited teaching a lesson

indicators.note: some of the following words means only part of their run of letters is used

parts.note: spans the end of the first word to the start of the last

explanation.surface: Someone praised a performance they quoted as being instructive.
explanation.definitionFit: Didactic describes something intended to instruct, often with a moral or moralising aim.

clue.text: The setter in Panama, say, and one Caribbean country

indicators.note: in places the setter's word inside the hat word

parts.note: a Panama is a kind of straw hat
the setter refers to themself as I
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: The setter visits Panama and another Caribbean nation.
explanation.walkthrough: Panama looks like the country, but here it is the straw hat.
explanation.definitionFit: Haiti is the nation occupying the western part of the island of Hispaniola in the Caribbean.

clue.text: Stopped Henry meeting Theodore

parts.note: Hal is a pet form of Henry, as with Shakespeare's Prince Hal
Ted is a short form of Theodore

explanation.surface: Henry's progress was halted when he ran into Theodore.
explanation.definitionFit: Halted means brought to a stop, the same past-tense verb sense.

clue.text: Soldier eccentrically accepting scouting mission

indicators.note: the phrase accepts the letters inside it, holding them across the gap between words

parts.note: spans the end of the first word to the start of the second

explanation.surface: An odd soldier agrees to go on a reconnaissance trip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eccentrically' looks like an anagram signal, but its letters are part of the hidden run.
explanation.definitionFit: Recce is British military slang, short for reconnaissance, an exploratory survey of ground.

clue.text: Steal heartless earl's cash abroad

parts.note: to nick is British slang for to steal

indicators.note: heartless means with the centre taken out, so only the ends of the word stay

parts.note: the word without its middle letters

explanation.surface: Someone pinches money from a nobleman travelling overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abroad' tells you the money is foreign: in the US and Canada a nickel is a five-cent coin.
explanation.definitionFit: A nickel is a coin worth five cents in America, so it is foreign money to a British solver.

clue.text: Enter taxi by home, a wooden hut

parts.note: to log is to enter in a record
a cab is a taxi
in means at home

explanation.surface: A traveller climbs into a taxi beside a house, heading for a wooden shelter.
explanation.definitionFit: A log cabin is a small dwelling built from tree trunks, a rustic timber shelter.

clue.text: Stick a knife in bananas from the east

indicators.note: in an across answer, starting from the east means reading right to left

parts.note: bananas and bats are both slang for crazy

explanation.surface: Someone plunges a blade into fruit shipped from the East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bananas' looks like fruit, but it means mad.
explanation.definitionFit: To stab is to thrust a pointed blade into something, the same verb sense.

clue.text: Give priestly approval to the grade below A minus

parts.note: in letter grades, B comes just after A
less means minus, as in ten less two

explanation.surface: A priest signs off a mark of B minus.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as the school grade B-minus, but 'minus' is a separate word to translate.
explanation.definitionFit: To bless is to invoke divine favour, as a priest does when consecrating someone or something.

clue.text: Black tails of woodpecker, skua, lapwing and crow

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils

indicators.note: a tail is the end, so each bird name gives up its final letter

parts.note: final letter
final letter
final letter

explanation.surface: A list of birds, ending with the crow, all seen from behind.
explanation.walkthrough: Crow sits among a list of birds, but it is the verb meaning boast.
explanation.definitionFit: To crow is to boast triumphantly, as a cockerel does, so the two verbs match.

clue.text: Kind of heron, for example, by river banks in Egypt

parts.note: e.g. is the abbreviation for for example
R is the abbreviation for river

indicators.note: banks are the edges of a river, so only the outer letters of the next word stay

parts.note: first and last letters

explanation.surface: A heron wades by the banks of a river in Egypt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'river banks' reads as one phrase about the Nile, but river gives one letter and banks acts on Egypt.
explanation.definitionFit: An egret is a white wading bird belonging to the heron family.

clue.text: Dissolute rake receiving a fine, singing in bars?

indicators.note: receiving means taking in, so further letters go inside
dissolute means loose and disorderly, so the next word is rearranged

parts.note: the four letters to be rearranged
taken as written
OK means fine

explanation.surface: A debauched man about town gets fined while crooning in pubs.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that bars are pubs, not musical bars.
explanation.definitionFit: Karaoke is amateur singing along to recorded backing tracks, typically in pubs and clubs.

clue.text: People who study biology GCSE toil so terribly

indicators.note: terribly means badly done, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: the ten letters of the three words

explanation.surface: Pupils sweat over their biology exam, working dreadfully hard.
explanation.walkthrough: A GCSE is the British exam taken at about sixteen; 'biology' seems to belong with it but ends the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecologists are scientists studying how living organisms relate to their environment, a branch of the life sciences.
